- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecasts are rising steadily, check for over-optimism — especially after recent supply events — and adjust downward if true outcomes show sharp spikes followed by mean reversion.
- If official event net supply is negative and bullish sentiment is low, model may underestimate downside risk — correct by adding a conservative downward bias to forecast.
- After a spike in price (e.g., >85), model often overestimates continuation — apply a “cool-down” rule: reduce forecast slope by 10–15% for next 3–5 periods.
- When sentiment is mixed or bearish (≤0.33) and model is rising, consider mean reversion bias — reduce forecast by 2–5% if recent price action shows no breakout.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if true outcome deviates >10% from model, check if sentiment history shows recent volatility — if yes, apply a “volatility dampening” rule: reduce forecast slope or add noise buffer.
- If official events show high bearish pressure (e.g., net supply > -20) and sentiment is weak, model may be overly bullish — apply a “bearish correction” rule: subtract 3–5% from forecast if price action is below 80.
- When multiple consecutive auctions (e.g., 3+ in 10d) are scheduled, model may overestimate supply impact — reduce forecast by 2–4% per auction unless sentiment is strongly bullish.
- If sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish cycles, model may be averaging — apply “cycle-aware” correction: adjust forecast based on recent sentiment direction (e.g., if last 3 days bearish, reduce forecast by 3–5%).
